extracted.intended_audience: readers of America's Future / general-interest media & culture commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and implicit criteria for judging the success or failure of late-night talk-show hosts and their programs, drawn from a critical opinion piece about Conan O’Brien and comparisons to peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience size / ratings matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A late-night show must draw a substantial real audience; social-media buzz cannot substitute for low viewership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article cites Conan drawing about one million viewers a night on TBS and contrasts this with disastrous Tonight Show numbers (less than three million viewers in summer 2009); notes that a $40 million payout followed the failure of the Tonight Show experiment. Anti-pattern: praising a host solely for "social media success" or "youth appeal" while ignoring weak ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create content people actually want to watch
rubrics_metrics.description: Success comes from producing unique, desirable products and programming rather than relying on marketing spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author credits Kimmel/Carolla with shows that "created unique products" (The Man Show, Crank Yankers) that "consumers ate up," while criticizing Conan for "re-packaging his same old routine." Guidance: prioritize original, watchable content over branding or narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Social media success" is not a replacement for viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of nebulous online or youth-oriented success (e.g., 'social media success' and 'youth appeal') do not offset poor TV ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article argues Conan’s bosses justify low ratings with "nebulous 'social media success' and 'youth appeal'." Example anti-pattern: treating cover-story puff pieces and web traffic as equivalent to audience engagement on the program itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / having a genuine reason to exist
rubrics_metrics.description: A host must have an authentic purpose or raison d'être for the show; ridiculing a format you created weakens that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: 'How can Conan ridicule the format of a show that he created himself? ... Separated from the standards and practices of the network TV behemoth, Conan not only lacks an edge. He lacks a reason to exist.' Anti-pattern: building a media brand around irony or mockery of one’s own format without offering substantive alternative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt content to the platform/format
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply transplanting a network-era show onto cable (or another platform) without substantive changes risks failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes Conan’s TBS hour is "virtually the same as his previous NBC efforts," implying insufficient adaptation. Guidance: retool format, pacing, and content to fit new platform constraints and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality and distinctiveness versus competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts must offer content or a perspective distinct from competitors (e.g., topical faux-newscasts, celebrity-magazine takedowns) to attract viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons: 'Why should we listen to Conan’s tired Mitt Romney jokes when we can watch Jon Stewart stage an entire faux-newscast? ... Who cares what Conan has to say about Kim Kardashian when Chelsea Handler is poring through each page of People magazine and Us Weekly?' Guidance: a host should differentiate their offering rather than repeat others’ angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective guest booking and handling B-list interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: A host must be able to make the most of the available guest pool and not rely on feigned boredom or shtick to carry interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article criticizes Conan’s habit of feigning boredom during B-list interviews and relying on it for laughs. Anti-pattern: tugs at collar when a monologue joke bombs or treating interviews as 'mandatory' rather than making them engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on celebrity cameos or star names
rubrics_metrics.description: Booking big-name guests does not automatically produce sustained ratings or a coherent product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Will Ferrell announcing Anchorman 2 on Conan was highlighted but author argues that big-money gets from mid-2000s stars do not equate to a successful, modern program. Guidance: guest appearances should serve a clear content strategy, not be the show's sole selling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-demographic fit and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts should cultivate a consistent audience and tone appropriate to that audience instead of awkwardly pandering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article says Conan’s audience shifted from 'jaded Gen-X ‘90s kids to pampered suburbanite millennials' due to youth-focused media strategy, which the author finds "repulsive to all but the lamest kinds of youth." Anti-pattern: forced pandering (staged same-sex marriage, name-dropping Salon) that signals manufactured attempts to attract demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resilience and strategic response to setbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: How a host responds to career setbacks and network conflicts matters — proactive, strategic moves can salvage or improve prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between Letterman (who obtained a CBS contract and succeeded) and Conan (who 'grew a beard and pouted' and pursued a live tour that 'wasn't all that funny'). Guidance: constructive, strategic responses (seek new contracts, reinvent format) are preferable to defeatist public displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainable comedic persona beyond network constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedic shtick that works as a network-born in-joke or as a reaction to constraints may not scale into an independent brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author: Conan's shtick 'was predicated solely on the fact that he had a job at NBC' and 'should have struck any fair-minded person as a terrible idea' to build a whole media entity around. Guidance: test whether persona stands on its own outside the original context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business credentials don't replace creative product
rubrics_metrics.description: A host's status, credentials, or business positioning (e.g., 'working for Turner') do not guarantee audience acceptance; the creative product must deliver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article mocks implied status ('Conan is a very important business executive who works for Turner') as irrelevant to ratings. Guidance: focus on content that viewers want, rather than relying on institutional imprimatur or PR narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid depending on marketing narratives and 'team' branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Branding campaigns and organized fan narratives (e.g., 'Team Coco') cannot substitute for a compelling nightly product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Piece references the 'Team Coco' branding and 'faux-populist liberal marketing campaigns' as insufficient to sustain a show. Example anti-pattern: using collective branding and press puff pieces to paper over a weak program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about what product is being sold
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful hosts can articulate or implicitly convey what the viewer is buying — humor style, perspective, or unique value — otherwise the show feels directionless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asks, 'What product, exactly, is Conan selling us for an hour a night four nights a week?' Guidance: ensure the show's format and content communicate a clear, sellable value proposition to viewers.
